    Distance-Based Mixed Models: Supported Designs and Validation

    distance-mixed-models.Rmd

    The package separates model compilation from inference. A formula first becomes a canonical Design Object. An inference engine then accepts that object only if it can state the hypothesis, EMS denominator, exchangeable units, permutation algorithm, and approximation status explicitly.

    Support boundaries

    Engine Supported design P-value
    permanova_oneway() One fixed grouping factor Raw-label permutation
    permanova_fixed() Sequential fixed effects Unrestricted raw-data permutation
    permanova_mixed() One balanced random intercept; fixed predictors constant within whole plots Whole-plot Freedman–Lane permutation
    permanova_nested() One balanced /-generated random-intercept hierarchy; each fixed term confined to one orthogonal hierarchy stratum Level-specific Freedman–Lane permutation within parents, moving descendants intact
    permanova_crossed() Complete equally replicated factorial with declared fixed-by-random components; permutation mode initially limited to one fixed treatment × one random block None by default; opt-in Euclidean Satterthwaite approximation or canonical within-block cell permutation

    Unsupported models fail instead of silently substituting a residual denominator or unrestricted permutation scheme.

    Balanced random-intercept model 

    generated <- simulate_balanced_mixed(
  groups_per_treatment = 3,
  replicates = 3,
  response_variables = 4,
  effect = 0.8,
  seed = 42
)

design <- compile_permanova_design(
  ~ treatment + (1 | site),
  data = generated$data,
  distance = generated$distance
)

fit <- permanova_mixed(design, permutations = 19, seed = 42)
fit
#> Distance-based balanced random-intercept model
#> Supported design: balanced single random intercept; fixed predictors constant within whole plots 
#> Permutation: term-specific Freedman-Lane whole-plot residual permutation 
#>                     term df        ss        ms                 denominator
#>                treatment  1  6.834214  6.834214 MS[site within fixed model]
#>  site within fixed model  4 72.883333 18.220833                        <NA>
#>              Within site 12 44.463747  3.705312                        <NA>
#>  denominator_df  pseudo_f p_perm
#>               4 0.3750769   0.95
#>              NA        NA     NA
#>              NA        NA     NA
fit$tests$treatment$symbolic_ems
#> $term
#> [1] "treatment"
#> 
#> $hypothesis
#> [1] "all estimable coefficients for `treatment` are zero"
#> 
#> $numerator_df
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $numerator_under_null

#>                1                3 
#> 
#> $numerator_under_alternative

#>                1                3                1 
#> 
#> $denominator
#>         residual random_intercept 
#>                1                3 
#> 
#> $denominator_term
#> [1] "site within fixed model"
#> 
#> $denominator_df
#> [1] 4
#> 
#> $exact_denominator
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $derivation
#> [1] "Both numerator and denominator contain sigma[e]^2 + 3 sigma[site]^2 under H0; the fixed-effect component occurs only in the numerator under H1."

    The numerator and whole-plot residual denominator both contain sigma[e]^2 + m sigma[site]^2 under the null. m is the number of observations per site. Permuting residuals as intact site blocks preserves the declared exchangeability structure.

    Non-Euclidean dissimilarities

    The complete centred spectrum is retained. No negative eigenvalue is silently removed.

    D <- matrix(c(0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 3, 1, 3, 0), 3, 3)
distance_diagnostics(D)[c("euclidean", "negative_count", "negative_inertia")]
#> $euclidean
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $negative_count
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $negative_inertia
#> [1] 0.8333333

    Corrections are not applied implicitly. Any future Lingoes, Cailliez, or square-root option must be reported as a separate sensitivity analysis.

    Operating-characteristic simulations distinguish a null location scenario, a location-shift power scenario, and a dispersion-heterogeneity scenario. Small runs are useful smoke tests only.

    simulation <- simulate_mixed_validation(
  simulations = 3,
  permutations = 19,
  seed = 42
)
simulation$summary
#>                   scenario              estimand simulations successful
#> 1                     null          type_I_error           3          3
#> 2           location_shift                 power           3          3
#> 3 dispersion_heterogeneity dispersion_robustness           3          3
#>   failures rejection_rate monte_carlo_se mean_p_value
#> 1        0              0              0    0.2833333
#> 2        0              0              0    0.3500000
#> 3        0              0              0    0.8166667
#>   max_abs_denominator_f_difference elapsed_seconds
#> 1                     2.664535e-15           0.015
#> 2                     2.664535e-15           0.010
#> 3                     9.063930e-16           0.011

    For scientific Type I error and power studies, increase both simulations and permutations, inspect Monte Carlo standard errors, and archive the settings with the results.

    Crossed models and variance components

    For balanced crossed models, EMS coefficients are calculated as tr(H Z Z') / df. Exact matching strata are pooled. If an exact match is not available, quasi_denominator() solves for an EMS-matched linear combination. Unrestricted variance components, including negative estimates, are primary; zero truncation is an optional sensitivity result.

    The standard fixed-treatment-by-random-block model declares its interaction component. That interaction mean square is then the exact treatment denominator.

    crossed_data <- expand.grid(
  replicate = factor(1:2),
  treatment = factor(c("control", "impact")),
  block = factor(1:6)
)
set.seed(42)
block_effect <- rnorm(6)
interaction_effect <- rnorm(12, sd = 2)
cell <- interaction(crossed_data$treatment, crossed_data$block, drop = TRUE)
crossed_response <- block_effect[crossed_data$block] +
  interaction_effect[cell] + rnorm(nrow(crossed_data))

crossed_design <- compile_permanova_design(
  ~ treatment + (1 | block) + (1 | treatment:block),
  crossed_data,
  dist(crossed_response)
)
crossed_fit <- permanova_crossed(crossed_design)
crossed_fit$tests$treatment$denominator
#> $expression
#> [1] "1*MS[treatment:block]"
#> 
#> $coefficients
#>           block treatment:block        Residual 
#>               0               1               0 
#> 
#> $ms
#> [1] 10.28956
#> 
#> $df
#> [1] 5
#> 
#> $pooled_strata
#> [1] "treatment:block"
#> 
#> $assumptions
#> character(0)

    Writing only (1 | block) omits the interaction variance and now fails by default. assume_additive = TRUE is available only as a deliberate model assumption; the result names both the assumed-zero component and every pooled denominator stratum. Satterthwaite p-values are suppressed when the compiled distance spectrum is non-Euclidean.

    interaction_validation <- simulate_crossed_interaction_validation(
  simulations = 10,
  blocks = 8,
  replicates = 3,
  seed = 42
)
interaction_validation$summary
#>                              method simulations rejected rejection_rate
#> 1              declared_interaction          10        0            0.0
#> 2 classical_interaction_denominator          10        0            0.0
#> 3      additive_opt_in_misspecified          10        1            0.1
#>   monte_carlo_se confidence_low confidence_high    mean_f
#> 1     0.00000000    0.000000000       0.3084971 0.3926929
#> 2     0.00000000    0.000000000       0.3084971 0.3926929
#> 3     0.09486833    0.002528579       0.4450161 1.7191414

    Scientific validation should use hundreds or thousands of simulations and interpret the reported binomial confidence intervals.

    Crossed randomized-block permutations

    For the canonical treatment-by-random-block design, complete replicated cells can be permuted among treatment positions separately within each block. This provides an empirical p-value for Euclidean or non-Euclidean distances while retaining the exact treatment-by-block EMS denominator.

    blocked_data <- expand.grid(
  replicate = factor(1:2), treatment = factor(c("a", "b")),
  block = factor(1:4)
)
set.seed(43)
blocked_cell <- interaction(
  blocked_data$treatment, blocked_data$block, drop = TRUE
)
blocked_response <- rnorm(4)[blocked_data$block] +
  rnorm(8)[blocked_cell] + rnorm(nrow(blocked_data), sd = 0.5)
blocked_design <- compile_permanova_design(
  ~ treatment + (1 | block) + (1 | treatment:block),
  blocked_data, dist(blocked_response)
)
blocked_fit <- suppressWarnings(permanova_crossed(
  blocked_design, p_method = "permutation", permutations = "all"
))
blocked_fit$tests$treatment[c(
  "statistic", "p_value", "permutation_algorithm",
  "attainable_permutations"
)]
#> $statistic
#> [1] 1.30079
#> 
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.375
#> 
#> $permutation_algorithm
#> [1] "raw permutation of intact `treatment:block` cells within `block`"
#> 
#> $attainable_permutations
#> [1] 16

    Additional fixed/random factors, nesting, imbalance, or an additive interaction omission remain outside this permutation envelope and fail explicitly.

    Balanced nested models

    permanova_nested() extends the exact whole-plot construction to one balanced random-intercept containment chain, such as (1 | region/site). Each fixed term is assigned to one orthogonal hierarchy stratum. Region effects move regions globally, site effects move complete sites within regions, and observation effects move observations within sites.

    nested_data <- expand.grid(
  replicate = factor(1:3), site = factor(1:2), region = factor(1:6)
)
nested_data$treatment <- factor(
  ifelse(as.integer(nested_data$region) <= 3, "control", "impact")
)
nested_data$site_treatment <- nested_data$site
nested_data$observation_treatment <- nested_data$replicate
set.seed(42)
nested_response <- rnorm(6)[nested_data$region] +
  rnorm(12)[interaction(nested_data$region, nested_data$site, drop = TRUE)] +
  rnorm(nrow(nested_data), sd = 0.5)
nested_design <- compile_permanova_design(
  ~ treatment + site_treatment + observation_treatment +
    (1 | region/site),
  nested_data, dist(nested_response)
)
nested_fit <- permanova_nested(nested_design, permutations = 19, seed = 42)
#> Warning: Only 64 permutations are attainable for hierarchy level `region:site`
#> (term(s): site_treatment); interpret p-values cautiously.
nested_fit$assignment_levels
#>             treatment        site_treatment observation_treatment 
#>              "region"         "region:site"         "observation"
lapply(nested_fit$tests, function(test) test$symbolic_ems$denominator)
#> $treatment
#>    residual      region region:site 
#>           1           6           3 
#> 
#> $site_treatment
#>      residual        region   region:site 
#>  1.000000e+00 -3.441691e-16  3.000000e+00 
#> 
#> $observation_treatment
#>      residual        region   region:site 
#>  1.000000e+00 -4.642751e-16 -4.693216e-16

    The engine rejects unequal hierarchy replication, crossed random terms, and a fixed hypothesis whose projector spans multiple levels. A within-site covariate with a non-zero between-site component must be decomposed into explicit between- and within-site hypotheses; the engine does not silently choose one.

    Reproducible benchmarks

    benchmark_permanova() returns machine-specific elapsed times. The installed script benchmarks/run-benchmarks.R provides a standard scaling grid. Timings should be reported with R version, platform, observation count, whole-plot count, and permutation count; the package makes no universal speed claim.
